question: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

The impact of the COVID‑19 vaccines continues to be a subject of controversy. While many scientific studies claim the vaccines proved beneficial in severe cases and helped ease pressure on the healthcare system, critics point to studies and analyses that cast doubt on the effectiveness and benefits of certain measures. The province of Lower Austria’s official COVID‑19 evaluation report presents data on how the pandemic developed in Austria. It shows that 94.2 % of all COVID‑19 infections between 11 March 2020 and 29 June 2023 occurred at the stage when 76.1 % of the population had been vaccinated. Furthermore, 74.1 % of all COVID‑19 deaths in Austria coincided with the vaccination campaign. Critics see this as an indication that, in spite of high vaccination rates, the vaccines failed to either prevent contagion or obstruct the spread of the virus. They are therefore calling for a comprehensive, transparent and independent review of pandemic policy – at European level too. In view of the EU’s common health strategy and the Commission’s role in vaccine procurement, questions have to be asked. 1.
Why does the Commission continue to spread information on the COVID‑19 vaccines that many consider to be incomplete or misleading?
Why does the Commission not do as the province of Lower Austria has done and acknowledge the possible missteps and shortcomings of the COVID‑19 vaccination strategy?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.8.2026) The Commission is committed to high standards of transparency and accountability. COVID19 vaccination is estimated to have saved millions of lives. The first year of vaccination alone was estimated to have halved the number of COVID-19 deaths across the world, resulting in 14 to 20 million lives saved1. The COVID-19 vaccines were authorised by the Commission following a scientific assessment of their quality, safety and efficacy and a recommendation for authorisation by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP). Based on these recommendations, the Commission prepared the decisions authorising the vaccines and consulted the Member States in the Standing Committee on Medicinal Products for Human Use before adoption. The vaccines were indicated for the prevention of serious disease caused by SARS-CoV-2 infection and not specifically authorised for the prevention of virus transmission. Real-world studies carried out afterwards, including large numbers of vaccinated people, concluded that COVID-19 vaccines can reduce the transmission of the virus2. Nonetheless, the effectiveness of the vaccines in preventing transmission was shown to be variable depending on time and country, reflecting the virus strains in circulation and the measures in place to reduce transmission. Information on COVID-19 vaccines and treatments is publicly available on EMA’s website3. In line with Article 168 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, while the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care is primarily a national competence, the Commission plays an important role in supporting, coordinating and complementing national action in the field of public health.
1 Global impact of the first year of COVID-19 vaccination: a mathematical modelling study - The Lancet
